c.tagline: Desert oasis capital of Peru's pisco and wine country, minutes from the palm-ringed Huacachina lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree on the fare before getting in, or use a ride-hailing app for a fixed price.

emergency.note: 116 is the fire brigade (Bomberos); response times outside Lima can be slower, especially at night.

avoid.reason: Petty theft around the bus terminals and Plaza de Armas at night; use registered taxis and keep valuables out of sight in Huacachina party hostels.

hood_desc: Ica's colonial-era heart, anchored by the cathedral and the Museo Regional de Ica's Paracas and Nazca artifacts; best for first-time visitors who want sights and dining within walking distance.
A palm-ringed desert lagoon minutes from downtown, surrounded by towering dunes and famed for dune-buggy rides and sandboarding; suits adventure travelers chasing sunset views.
A quiet traditional neighborhood tied to local legends of witches (brujas), with small family-run eateries; good for travelers wanting an authentic, low-key feel.
A rural district on Ica's outskirts home to pisco and wine bodegas like El Catador, with tasting tours through vineyards; suits travelers interested in Peru's pisco heritage.
Countryside district holding Bodega Tacama, one of the oldest wineries in South America, amid vineyards and open desert scenery; good for wine tourism and a slower pace.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap water is not potable.

transit.hours: Mototaxis and combis run roughly 6 AM to 10-11 PM; taxis and ride apps cover late night.
transit.pay: Cash paid directly to the driver; mototaxi fares are negotiated and combis charge a fixed per-route amount, generally 1-3 soles within the city.
transit.note: Ica has no metro or formal bus network; mototaxis are the primary way to get around, with combis linking Ica to Huacachina and surrounding towns.

bus: Cruz del Sur, Oltursa, and other intercity buses to Lima and Nazca

tip.r: Not obligatory; some restaurants add a 10% service charge automatically, in which case an extra tip isn't expected, otherwise rounding up or 10% is appreciated.

food.name: Carapulcra
food.desc: Ica's emblem dish: sun-dried potatoes rehydrated and simmered with pork, aji panca, peanut and cloves into a dark, deeply savoury stew.

places.name: Restaurante El Intipalka
places.note: Vineyard restaurant serving carapulcra with three meats alongside its own wines.

places.name: Tacama
places.note: South America's oldest vineyard; its restaurant plates the classic carapulcra con sopa seca.

places.name: La Olla de Juanita
places.note: Family criollo kitchen with live music at weekends and a black carapulcra worth ordering.

food.name: Sopa Seca
food.desc: Despite the name, a dry noodle dish: thin pasta stained red with aji and tomato, heavy with basil and coriander, served pressed against carapulcra.

places.name: Tacama
places.note: Serves the traditional manchapecho pairing of sopa seca with carapulcra.

places.name: La Olla de Juanita
places.note: Generous criollo portions at local prices rather than tour-group rates.

places.name: Mercado Modelo de Ica
places.note: Market comedor stalls plate sopa seca at breakfast and lunch for a few soles.

food.name: Picante de Pallares
food.desc: Large creamy lima beans grown in the Ica valley, stewed with aji, garlic and cheese into a rich, mild picante served with rice.

places.name: Tacama
places.note: Regional menu includes picante de pallares served with beef tenderloin.

places.name: Mercado Modelo de Ica
places.note: The place to eat pallares the way iquenos do, and to buy the dried beans.

places.name: La Olla de Juanita
places.note: Rotating criollo dailies that lean on the valley's beans and dried potatoes.

food.name: Tejas
food.desc: Ica's signature sweet: pecans, dried fruit or lucuma wrapped in manjar blanco and sealed in a snow-white sugar fondant shell.

places.name: Helena Chocolates y Tejas
places.note: The city's best-known teja maker since the 1940s, with a factory shop and tastings.

places.name: Bodega El Catador
places.note: Classic pisco bodega stop that sells tejas and chocotejas alongside its spirits.

places.name: Plaza de Armas de Ica shops
places.note: The main square is ringed by dulcerias selling boxed tejas to take away.

food.name: Chocotejas
food.desc: The chocolate-coated cousin of the teja, filled with manjar blanco and pecan, fig or pisco-soaked raisin; the standard gift from Ica.

places.name: Helena Chocolates y Tejas
places.note: Long-established maker turning out dozens of chocoteja fillings daily.

places.name: Bodega El Catador
places.note: Pairs pisco tastings with pisco-filled chocotejas.

places.name: Huacachina lagoon shops
places.note: Oasis stalls stock chocotejas for visitors coming off the dune buggies.

food.name: Frijol Colado
food.desc: A dark, glossy pudding of strained black beans cooked down with sugar, cloves and sesame seeds, an old Afro-Peruvian dessert of the coast.

places.name: Mercado Modelo de Ica
places.note: Sweet vendors sell it by the cup, freshly made, near the fruit aisles.

places.name: La Olla de Juanita
places.note: Keeps the older Afro-Peruvian desserts on the menu, not just the tourist ones.

places.name: Plaza de Armas de Ica shops
places.note: Traditional dulcerias around the square carry frijol colado in season.

food.name: Pisco
food.desc: Peru's grape brandy, born in this valley; try it neat as puro quebranta or shaken into a pisco sour with lime, egg white and bitters.

places.name: Bodega El Catador
places.note: The classic Ica bodega visit: free tastings across pisco styles plus a restaurant.

places.name: Bodega Vista Alegre
places.note: Founded in 1857 and one of Peru's oldest working wineries, with daily tours.

places.name: Tacama
places.note: Historic hacienda estate pouring both pisco and wine with vineyard views.

food.name: Cachina
food.desc: Cloudy, barely fermented grape must drunk young and sweet during the March harvest; a strictly local Ica speciality you rarely see in Lima.

places.name: Bodega El Catador
places.note: Sells cachina and pisco-based cocktails during and after the grape harvest.

places.name: Bodega Lazo
places.note: Small artisanal bodega in an old colonial house known for traditional cachina.

places.name: Mercado Modelo de Ica
places.note: Drinks vendors sell cachina by the glass in harvest season, straight from the jug.

landmarks: Huacachina Oasis
A palm-fringed desert lagoon ringed by giant dunes, where sandboarding and roaring buggy rides make Peru's dream oasis unforgettable.
Museo Regional de Ica
A remarkable regional museum of Paracas textiles, elongated skulls and Nazca ceramics that unlocks southern Peru's pre-Columbian mysteries.
Ica Cathedral
An 18th-century Jesuit-founded cathedral on the Plaza de Armas, its neoclassical facade and refined wooden interior surviving repeated earthquakes.
Plaza de Armas de Ica
The palm-shaded heart of the city, ringed by colonial arcades, an obelisk fountain and the everyday bustle of Iqueño life.
Santuario del Señor de Luren
Ica's most venerated church, rebuilt after earthquakes, whose Lord of Luren image draws enormous candlelit processions every October.
Bodega Tacama
South America's oldest winery, a rose-colored colonial hacienda offering tastings of pisco and wine amid vineyards first planted in the 1540s.
Bodega El Catador
A traditional family distillery where visitors watch grapes trodden and pisco distilled in copper stills before generous tasting rounds.
Cachiche (village of the witches)
A legendary hamlet of healers just outside Ica, famous for its witch monument and a seven-headed palm wrapped in local prophecy.
Cañón de los Perdidos (Canyon of the Lost)
A hidden desert canyon of wind-sculpted walls and dramatic gorges, Ica's most surprising day-trip discovery deep in the Ocucaje desert.
Paracas National Reserve and Ballestas Islands
A day-trip-able coastal reserve of red-sand beaches and wildlife-packed islands teeming with sea lions, penguins and boobies.

train.note: Ica has no railway. Peru's surviving passenger services are the Cusco lines to Machu Picchu run by PeruRail (https://www.perurail.com/) and Inca Rail (https://incarail.com/), the Ferrocarril Central Andino from Lima to Huancayo, and the short international Tacna-Arica line into Chile - none of them comes anywhere near the south coast. Getting to Ica therefore means a bus down the Panamericana Sur, which is fast, frequent and much cheaper than flying.

bus.note: Ica is about 4-5 hours from Lima and 2-3 hours from Nazca, with departures throughout the day and evening. Soyuz/PeruBus (https://www.soyuz.pe/) runs the cheap high-frequency shuttle from Lima's Avenida México terminal every 10-15 minutes, while Cruz del Sur (https://www.cruzdelsur.com.pe/) and Oltursa (https://www.oltursa.pe/) offer the more comfortable reclining-seat coaches from their own terminals; in Ica the companies use separate offices along Avenida Municipalidad and the Panamericana rather than a single station. Huacachina is a 10-minute taxi from the terminals. No international coaches serve Ica - Cruz del Sur and Ormeño's services to Chile, Bolivia, Ecuador and Argentina all start in Lima.

ferry.note: Ica sits inland in a desert valley about 50 km from the sea, and Peru has no scheduled coastal passenger ferries; the nearest boats are the Ballestas Islands tour launches from Paracas, roughly an hour away, which are sightseeing excursions rather than transport.

half.name: Pisco
half.blurb: A port town where Peru's grape brandy takes its name, with waterfront wineries and boat departures for the Ballestas Islands, about ninety minutes from Ica.

half.name: Chincha (El Carmen)
half.blurb: An Afro-Peruvian cultural center known for its percussion music and dance traditions, roughly two hours north of Ica.

full.name: Nazca Lines
full.blurb: Massive geoglyphs etched into the desert floor, best seen from a small overflight plane, about two and a half hours south of Ica.
